The Iron Curtain. The metaphorical and literal barrier separating communist Eastern Europe from Western Europe during the Cold War. The term, popularized by Winston Churchill in nineteen forty-six, described the ideological, political, and physical divisions established by the Soviet Union across the continent after World War II. The Iron Curtain symbolized the division of Europe into two hostile blocs and remained the defining symbol of Cold War division until its collapse in nineteen eighty-nine. The term emerged from Churchill's "Sinews of Peace" speech in March nineteen forty-six, warning that "an iron curtain has descended across the Continent"—a vivid metaphor that captured Western fears of permanent Soviet dominance of Eastern Europe. The Iron Curtain represented both an ideological divide between communism and capitalism and physical barriers: the Berlin Wall, barbed wire fences, anti-tank obstacles, electrified fences, and heavily militarized borders guarded by armed soldiers under shoot-on-sight orders. The Soviet Union established satellite states across Eastern Europe—Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, and East Germany—subordinating them to Moscow's control through military occupation, communist puppet governments, and secret police including the Stasi and Securitate that surveilled populations. Travel restrictions accompanied the Iron Curtain. Citizens were largely prevented from moving between East and West, with families separated for decades. Escape attempts meant risking death from border guards—thousands died trying to cross the Iron Curtain. The Berlin Wall, constructed in nineteen sixty-one, became the physical embodiment of the Iron Curtain, symbolizing the division of Europe and the world. It ran ninety-six miles through Berlin, separating the city and demonstrating the desperation of the Cold War. Economic disparity grew as Western European economies thrived under capitalism and Marshall Plan aid while Soviet-dominated Eastern Europe stagnated under central planning, resource extraction to benefit the USSR, and repression of entrepreneurship and innovation. The Iron Curtain dissolved with the collapse of communism from nineteen eighty-nine to nineteen ninety-one. The Berlin Wall fell in November nineteen eighty-nine. Soviet satellites gained independence—Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, and Bulgaria. The Soviet Union collapsed in nineteen ninety-one. The ideological barrier dissolved as Russia itself transformed.
